rubric.why: Award for the textbook definition of oxidation.
rubric.description: Oxidation is the gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen.
rubric.how: Look for either correct definition of oxidation.

rubric.why: Award for the contrasting definition of reduction.
rubric.description: Reduction is the loss of oxygen or gain of hydrogen.
rubric.how: Look for either correct definition of reduction.

modelAnswer: Oxidation is the gain of oxygen or loss of hydrogen.
Reduction is the loss of oxygen or gain of hydrogen.

items.followUp: Write the balanced chemical equation for photosynthesis.

rubric.why: The equation must show the correct reactants and products in balanced proportions.
rubric.how: Award full marks for the balanced equation; award one mark if the substances are correct but the equation is not balanced.

items.followUp: What is meant by aerobic respiration?

rubric.why: The defining feature of anaerobes is their ability to live without oxygen.
rubric.description: States that anaerobes live in the absence of oxygen.
rubric.how: Look for a clear statement that they can live without oxygen.

rubric.why: The answer must identify anaerobes as organisms.
rubric.how: Award for naming them as organisms that live without oxygen.

modelAnswer: Anaerobes are organisms that can live in the absence of oxygen.

items.followUp: Define heterotrophic organisms and give one example.

rubric.why: Autotrophs are defined by their ability to make their own food.
rubric.description: States that autotrophs make their own food.
rubric.how: Look for a clear description of self-nutrition.

rubric.why: A correct example completes the answer.
rubric.description: Gives a valid example of an autotroph.
rubric.how: Accept green plants, grass, algae, or another correct example.

modelAnswer: Autotrophic organisms make their own food from simple inorganic substances.

items.followUp: State two functions of roots in a plant.

rubric.why: Stomata allow gases to move between the plant and its surroundings.
rubric.description: States that stomata enable gaseous exchange.
rubric.how: Look for the exchange of gases through stomata.

rubric.why: Stomata also provide an outlet for water vapour during transpiration.
rubric.description: States that stomata enable transpiration or water-vapour loss.
rubric.how: Look for transpiration or loss of water vapour.

modelAnswer: Stomata allow gaseous exchange between the plant and its surroundings.
They also allow water vapour to escape during transpiration.

items.followUp: What are stomata, and what is their function?

rubric.why: Lenticels are openings in the plant surface.
rubric.description: Identifies lenticels as small openings or pores.
rubric.how: Look for a description of lenticels as openings or pores.

rubric.why: Their location in woody plant parts is required.
rubric.description: States that lenticels are found in the bark or stems, especially woody stems.
rubric.how: Look for bark or stem as the location.

modelAnswer: Lenticels are small openings in the bark of woody plants.
They are found on woody stems and allow gaseous exchange.

items.followUp: Explain the tissue and cell levels of organization, with an example of each.

rubric.why: An organ consists of different tissues working together to carry out a particular function.
rubric.description: Defines an organ and explains that its tissues work together for a function.
rubric.how: Award one mark for the combination of different tissues and one for their coordinated function.

rubric.why: An organ system is made up of organs that work together to perform major functions.
rubric.description: Defines an organ system as organs working together.
rubric.how: Award one mark for identifying a group of organs and one for their coordinated function.

rubric.why: An appropriate example demonstrates the levels of organization.
rubric.description: Gives a correct example of an organ or organ system.
rubric.how: Accept an organ such as a leaf or heart, or an organ system such as the digestive system.

modelAnswer: An organ is a structure made of different tissues working together to perform a particular function; for example, a leaf is a plant organ.
An organ system is a group of organs working together to perform major functions of the body.
For example, the stomach and other digestive organs work together in the digestive system.

items.followUp: Describe the structure and function of ribosomes.

rubric.why: The endoplasmic reticulum is a network of membranes in the cell.
rubric.description: Describes the ER as a membrane network.
rubric.how: Look for a membrane network or system of membranes.

rubric.why: Rough ER is distinguished by ribosomes on its surface.
rubric.description: Identifies rough ER and its ribosomes.
rubric.how: Award for stating that ribosomes are attached to rough ER.

rubric.why: Rough ER is associated with protein synthesis.
rubric.description: Gives the role of rough ER in protein synthesis.
rubric.how: Look for protein production or synthesis.

rubric.why: Smooth ER lacks ribosomes and is associated with lipid synthesis.
rubric.description: Identifies smooth ER and a distinguishing feature or function.
rubric.how: Award for stating that smooth ER lacks ribosomes or synthesizes lipids.

modelAnswer: The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is a network of membranes in the cytoplasm.
Rough endoplasmic reticulum has ribosomes attached to its surface and is involved in protein synthesis.
Smooth endoplasmic reticulum has no ribosomes attached.
Smooth ER is involved in lipid synthesis.
